segments.text: Have you ever read a passage in English class that required two or three attempts to actually
understand?
You read the words, but your brain has to work through them in multiple passes before
the logic snaps into place.
This diagram illustrates a classic grammatical puzzle.
Try reading the sentence out loud.
The horse raced past the barn.
Fell.
On a first read, the sentence feels broken.
You reach the final word, and it seems to stop short.
It feels as if a word was left out.
So you read it again.
You start testing different possibilities against the grammar.
You have to decide if a barn fell down or if the horse was the one that fell after running past it.
The structure finally resolves.
Someone raced a horse past a barn, and then the horse fell.
In this context, raced describes the horse, and fell is the action the horse took.
Each read updates the meaning until it clicks.
AI does something similar.
It builds meaning through repeated updates.
AI doesn't read your message the way you do.
Instead of reading left to right like a human, an AI processes your text through a physical
series of computational layers.
This diagram shows how those layers are structured.
The entire sequence, from the input side to the output side, represents a single architecture.
The whole stack of layers is called a neural network.
Inside every individual layer, two steps work together to help the system figure out
what your words mean in context.
Attention and transformation update the numbers at each layer.
The movement is continuous.
Numbers enter on the left, pass through a long line of layers to undergo successive updates,
and emerge as final numbers on the far right.
Let's track two specific numbers out of the many on this board.
They enter the system at 0.42 and negative 1.15.
By the time they reach the end, they have shifted to 0.19 and negative 1.12.
This mathematical movement provides the mechanism for determining how a specific word fits into
a real sentence.
We can see this in action by resolving an ambiguous pronoun.
The sentence is, the cat sat on the mat during the May rainstorm because it was tired.
We need to figure out what the word it refers to.
In the starting block, the numerical values for the word it, like 0.12 and negative 0.34,
do not indicate a specific subject.
As the numbers move into layer 1, the first set of updates begins to capture a loose connection
between the word it and the word cat.
In layer 2, the updated numbers carry more detailed information, strengthening that specific
connection further.
This cycle continues through many more passes.
Each layer builds entirely on the mathematical output provided by the previous one.
By the final block, the numbers arrive at their destination values of 0.41 and 0.06.
AI works out that it refers to cat.
The system doesn't have an internal definition of what a cat is.
Instead, these sequential updates align the numbers to point directly at the subject,
solving the contextual puzzle.
Untangling a single pronoun or a confusing sentence about a horse requires a few passes,
but untangling sarcasm, story twists, or multi-step reasoning requires significantly more work.
To solve those harder problems, modern AI models operate at a massive scale.
They use dozens and sometimes over 100 layers, giving the system enough discrete steps
to map out complex relationships.
However, we cannot simply add layers infinitely.
Every additional layer requires more computing power and more processing time.
The extra benefit has to be worth the cost.
The entire system relies on the slow, sequential accumulation of context.
Meaning builds up layer by layer.
Attention and transformation.
Dozens of times.
